prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reached fractional frequency uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I move my preferred configuration from B049 to B030, and I want to give the reason on scientific grounds and not because six colleagues have gathered there. The chair asked whether the KPZ minority still holds after the attribution arguments. My own round-1 objection has not been answered: the 1986 paper has three authors, Parisi is one of them and is already a laureate, and the credited names for B049 would therefore split the original paper in a way I cannot defend as the discoverers' credit. Spohn's exact-solution programme is a different and later achievement, so adding him does not repair the problem. The lattice clock, by contrast, has the property I look for: a simple mechanism, the magic wavelength at which ground and clock states share the same polarizability so that the trapping light stops shifting the transition, followed by a rigorous treatment of every systematic (blackbody, collisional, lattice light shifts) until independent clocks in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere agree near 1e-18. The idea is understood, not merely effective, and the attribution to Katori for the proposal and first demonstration and to Ye for the accuracy and many-body regime is accepted by every member who proposed laureates. I still regard KPZ as the scientifically most universal result on the list, so it remains my first alternative.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection is real. Frequency combs (2005) and the control of single quantum systems including the Al+ ion clock (2012) sit next to this work, and a strict reading of discovery or invention could call the lattice clock a refinement. I think the magic-wavelength scheme is a distinct idea, since it solves the light-shift problem for many neutral atoms at once, but it is a judgement and not a proof. Early contributors such as Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley are outside a two-name credit, and the most visible payoffs (redefinition of the second, dark-matter and constants searches) are still prospective. Finally, my move is partly driven by an attribution defect in my own first choice, so B030 is the best available configuration and not necessarily a better piece of physics than KPZ.

responses.point: Asks whether a citation can separate the lattice clock from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes and how to divide credit between Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I agree and I would answer your first question in the wording itself: the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realization at the 1e-18 level, and not frequency metrology in general. On the split, I read Katori as the originator of the concept and first demonstration and Ye as the one who established the accuracy and many-body regime; neither half is separable from the other, which is why I accept a two-name prize and do not want early groups listed as if they were co-laureates. I can only treat Lemonde's group as a discussion point for the expert report, not as a reason to change the names.

responses.point: Asks whether a precision-measurement record counts as a discovery or invention in the statutory sense, and wants the citation kept narrow and free of applications.
responses.response: I side with your narrow citation. The statute covers invention as well as discovery, and the magic-wavelength condition is a conceptual step, not just a better instrument. I would still keep the SI redefinition and clock geodesy out of the citation, because they are prospective, and I would defend the prize on what has been shown: independent clocks agreeing near 1e-18. Your Tokyo fellowship does not seem to me to create a conflict, since you report no tie to Katori or Ye, but that is for the committee to decide.

responses.point: Says the original 1986 KPZ paper includes Parisi, who is absent from the credited names and already a 2021 laureate, making a fair KPZ prize difficult to construct, and keeps B058 as first alternative.
responses.response: You are right, and this is the main reason I have moved off B049. I had acknowledged the issue in my round-1 citation, but a citation cannot repair a prize list that omits a co-author of the founding paper. On B058 I still agree that the quantum spin Hall effect is original and robust, but the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for the HgTe prediction is the same kind of defect, so I keep it as a second alternative and not as my lead.

responses.point: Concedes that precision CMB mapping (B055) rests on a WMAP versus Planck and Page versus Puget allocation problem, and says he would not be unhappy to see B030 win.
responses.response: Your concession is a fair summary of why B055 and B049 have the same shape: a deep scientific case with a name problem that cannot be repaired within three people. I do not think this is a sign that cosmology is less deserving, only that the three-name limit bites harder on satellite collaborations. I accept the discovery is mature and independently confirmed; my disagreement is only that I cannot choose a trio I would defend, so I did not rank it above B030.

responses.point: Argues the lattice clock is a genuinely new idea resting on atomic polarizability physics, reproduced across several laboratories, though she discloses that she is close to the field and may be biased upward.
responses.response: Your round-1 point on polarizability is the part I find most persuasive, since the whole scheme reduces to one clean condition that can be calculated and then checked. Because you disclose closeness to the field, I would ask you to say plainly whether any of the early priority claims (Lemonde, Takamoto, Hinkley) has substance for you as an expert. That is the question that most affects whether two names are enough, and I cannot judge it from the outside.

responses.point: Moved from IceCube to B030 as the consensus prize, but cannot settle priority in atomic physics and finds no second distinct part that works within three people.
responses.response: I agree that no second part fits cleanly. B020 and B058 each need names beyond the shortlist trios or a choice among many contributors, and adding either to a two-person B030 would exceed three people unless one name were dropped, which I do not think is fair to either part. A single-part B030 prize is therefore my proposal, and I would not add B049 as a second part, since the Parisi problem remains.

uncertainties: Whether expert reviewers find a priority claim (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley) strong enough to change the Katori and Ye credit.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a prize-level invention distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes, which turns on the wording of the citation.

Whether a KPZ prize could ever be defended without Parisi, and whether Spohn's later exact solutions belong to the same achievement; I think not, but I have not tested this with a mathematical physicist.
Whether the HgTe attribution for B058 could be repaired within three people, which determines whether it should be my lead in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I have no recorded collaboration with Katori, Ye, Kardar, Zhang, Spohn or any other credited name, and I am not in the atomic-clock field. I note only that I am in the Gothenburg physics environment alongside Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers); that is institutional proximity and not a conflict, and I see no reason to recuse myself on B030.
